title: Find culinary strengths that suit your home or occasion
intro: Private chefs in Dubai bring different cooking interests, experience and approaches to service. The most useful way to explore a directory is to connect those strengths with your own brief. A family cooking plan, a hands-on lesson and a multi-course dinner ask different things of a professional. Use the profiles as a starting point, then discuss the actual menu, dates and kitchen with myCHEF. We can assess a proposed match against the work you want done and confirm the arrangement before you book.

sections.title: Read a profile with your own menu in mind
paragraphs: Look for a relevant cooking direction, then ask how it would translate into your service. If a profile interests you because of Italian dishes, explain whether you want a pasta lesson, weekly family meals or a hosted dinner. Those are different briefs even when the cuisine is similar.

Availability needs to be checked for your dates, and the final menu should suit the proposed chef and setting. A profile is an introduction to a possible direction, not a guarantee that every dish or schedule can be provided. Share your priorities so the recommendation can be specific.

sections.title: Look for a chef whose strengths fit the brief
paragraphs: A chef who excels at an elaborate tasting menu may not be the best match for a household that wants simple daily meals and careful batch preparation. Start with the work you actually need: particular cuisines, family cooking, confident service for guests or a regular routine with multiple meals. Relevant experience matters more than a list of impressive-sounding dishes.

Discuss the proposed chef's approach to your kitchen and schedule. How would the menu fit the available hours? Which dishes work well for later meals? What information would they need before the first visit? These practical questions make an introduction more useful than a general conversation about favourite food.

myCHEF considers the brief alongside availability when recommending a match. Profiles can help you understand cooking interests and service styles, but the proposed arrangement still needs confirmation. If you would like a paid trial or tasting, agree the purpose, menu and price first so you know exactly what you will be assessing.

sections.title: Translate a favourite cuisine into a focused brief
paragraphs: A cuisine name opens the conversation, but particular dishes and flavours help a chef understand what you mean. Italian might suggest handmade pasta to one household and grilled fish with simple vegetables to another. Middle Eastern cooking can mean a relaxed mezze table, regional home-style dishes or a more formal sequence. Share examples rather than expecting one label to communicate every preference.

Mention the intensity of flavour you enjoy, preferred ingredients and any dishes that have personal significance. If your household likes several cuisines, discuss how they should appear across the week or within an occasion. Variety can work beautifully when the menu has a clear structure and does not ask the kitchen to produce too many unrelated preparations at once.

Ask the proposed chef which parts of the brief best match their experience. A candid conversation about strengths is more useful than promising every possible dish. The resulting menu should feel personal while remaining realistic for the available time, equipment and service format.

sections.title: Give a trial or tasting a clear purpose
paragraphs: A trial is most useful when it resembles the work you want the chef to do. For household cooking, that might mean preparing a realistic family meal and a dish for later. For an occasion, a tasting may focus on selected menu items rather than reproducing the whole event. Explain what you want to assess before deciding the format.

Consider flavour, organisation, communication and how comfortably the food fits your preferences. An elaborate dish can be impressive without demonstrating the everyday cooking you need. Equally, a small tasting cannot show every aspect of service for a larger group, where staffing, equipment and timing introduce different demands.

Any cooking trial or tasting needs an agreed menu, location, duration and price. Ingredients, preparation and travel still involve work even for a small number of people. Afterwards, give clear feedback and discuss any changes before confirming a longer arrangement or final event menu. A successful trial is a useful decision point, not an automatic commitment.

sections.title: Ask about checks that relate to the proposed work
paragraphs: When assessing a chef service, ask questions that help you understand the person and arrangement being proposed. Relevant cooking experience, identity and work eligibility, references and food handling awareness all serve different purposes. A profile description alone does not answer every question about suitability for your household.

Discuss how practical ability is considered alongside documentation. You may want experience with a particular cuisine, confidence in a domestic kitchen or an organised approach to recurring preparation. The best evidence is connected to those needs, rather than a long list of credentials that may have little bearing on the work you are booking.

If a requirement is essential, raise it before confirming the match. Ask what information can be shared and how a specific concern will be addressed. Checks support an informed decision, but they do not remove the need for a clear brief, suitable kitchen conditions and ongoing feedback. A thoughtful introduction brings those parts together before the service begins.

sections.title: Give every person in the service a clear role
paragraphs: Cooking, carrying plates, pouring drinks and clearing a table are different jobs. For a quiet household visit, you may need only a chef. For an occasion with several courses or guests arriving together, an assistant or service professional can help the kitchen and dining area run at the right pace. Staffing should follow the work, rather than a fixed assumption based only on headcount.

Discuss who will greet guests, replenish water, serve each course and clear used plates. If the chef is expected to do all of those tasks while cooking, the menu and timing need to allow for it. Extra support can be especially useful when the kitchen is far from the dining table or the meal involves several dietary variations.

Your proposal should identify the included roles and service hours. Additional hospitality, equipment and event coordination should be agreed as part of the scope. That clarity lets everyone focus on their responsibilities and gives you a more relaxed experience as host.

sections.title: Make the first visit a useful foundation
paragraphs: For the first visit, choose a menu that gives the chef a realistic picture of your household. Include food you know well enough to give useful feedback on, rather than making every dish unfamiliar. Keep the priorities clear: which meal matters most, what should be prepared for later and what time the kitchen needs to be ready.

Allow a short introduction to the space. Show the chef the appliances, utensils, storage areas and any items that need special care. Confirm the grocery arrangements and clarify which household member should answer questions if you are unavailable. This helps prevent small uncertainties from interrupting the cooking repeatedly.

At the end, review the practical handover as well as the food. Know which dishes are ready to eat, which need finishing and what instructions apply to them. Then share feedback on portions, taste and timing. The first visit is an opportunity to make the next one more precise, comfortable and useful for everyone involved.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
